clinicalPearls: Myocardial iron deposition may arise from hereditary haemochromatosis (typically HFE C282Y homozygosity) or from secondary/transfusional iron overload (thalassaemia major, sideroblastic anaemia, myelodysplasia); the secondary forms often cause the most severe cardiac disease because transfused iron bypasses regulatory absorption controls.

The cardiomyopathy characteristically evolves through an early restrictive/diastolic phase into a later dilated phase with systolic impairment, so a normal ejection fraction does not exclude significant iron loading.
Iron preferentially accumulates in ventricular myocardium and the conduction system, producing a mixed picture of heart failure plus atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and heart block.

Cardiac T2* magnetic resonance is the pivotal non-invasive tool: a myocardial T2* below the accepted threshold identifies clinically important iron loading before ejection fraction falls, and it guides intensification of chelation.
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation reflect total body iron but correlate poorly with myocardial iron, so cardiac assessment must not rely on ferritin alone.

Iron-related cardiac dysfunction is substantially reversible if chelation (or venesection in primary disease) is instituted before end-stage fibrosis develops, distinguishing it from most other restrictive cardiomyopathies.
In transfusion-dependent patients, combining or intensifying iron chelators for cardiac indications can recover ventricular function and reduce arrhythmic death.
Coexisting endocrinopathy (diabetes, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism) and hepatic disease frequently accompany the cardiomyopathy and worsen overall prognosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Excess iron, whether from dysregulated intestinal absorption in hereditary haemochromatosis or from repeated transfusion, saturates transferrin and circulates as non-transferrin-bound iron that is taken up by cardiomyocytes largely through L-type and T-type calcium channels. Intracellular labile iron catalyses Fenton-type generation of reactive oxygen species, causing lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial injury and impaired excitation-contraction coupling. Iron is deposited within lysosomes and myofibrils, initially stiffening the ventricle and impairing relaxation (a restrictive physiology), and later provoking myocyte loss and replacement fibrosis that culminate in ventricular dilatation and systolic failure. Iron loading of the sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node and conducting tissue underlies the associated bradyarrhythmias, heart block and atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.
additionalInvestigations: cardiac magnetic resonance with myocardial T2* mapping
HFE genotyping (C282Y, H63D) in suspected hereditary disease
echocardiography with diastolic and tissue Doppler assessment
ambulatory ECG monitoring for arrhythmia and conduction disease
liver iron quantification (MRI R2/R2*) and liver function tests
endocrine screen including fasting glucose, thyroid and gonadal axes
redFlags: new or progressive heart failure in a transfusion-dependent patient
high-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia
falling ejection fraction with markedly reduced myocardial T2*
rapid decompensation suggesting advanced iron-related systolic failure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is favourable when iron overload is detected and treated before irreversible fibrosis, with substantial recovery of ventricular function and rhythm; established dilated systolic failure or advanced conduction disease carries high morbidity and mortality, and cardiac iron loading remains a leading cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia.
pitfalls: relying on serum ferritin, which does not reliably reflect myocardial iron burden
assuming a normal ejection fraction excludes dangerous iron loading
attributing arrhythmia or heart block to other causes and missing reversible iron toxicity
under-dosing or delaying chelation once cardiac involvement is evident
overlooking secondary transfusional overload because HFE testing is negative
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
Thalassaemia International Federation guidelines for management of transfusion-dependent thalassaemia
